extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science; readers of philosophy of science and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what counts as scientific knowledge, how to practise quantitative (statistical) science, and criteria/principles for classifying the sciences (discussing Bacon, Comte, Spencer and practical measurement examples in evolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Science is description not explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is essentially a description and not an explanation — the object of science is to describe in conceptual shorthand the routine of our past experience, with a view of predicting our future experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the psychological standpoint scientific work is association; from the physical standpoint it is the development of excitatory connections. Conceptions are ideal symbols (conceptual shorthand) formed from stored sense-impresses and used to index perceptions. Emphasises predictive power rather than metaphysical explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace complex descriptions by simpler formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of the naturalist is to replace longer and more complex descriptions by more comprehensive and simpler descriptions — to discover in variation, growth, and heredity facts which can be described by a few formulae, nay, if possible, by one brief formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages seeking compact quantitative laws to summarise phenomena; motivates the application of mathematical/statistical summaries to biological data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base science on sense-impressions and association
rubrics_metrics.description: The contents of the mind take their origin in sense-impressions and in our modes of perceiving sense-impressions; conceptions are formed from stored sense-impresses by association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits material for classification (e.g., excluding natural theology and metaphysics) and grounds scientific classification in perceptual/experiential material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantitative/statistical methods with physicist-like accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative methods — as accurate as those of the physicist — are being applied to life; the statistical method indicates in most cases a direct plan of attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires careful experiments and observation to indicate rates (e.g., rapidity of natural selection); gives examples (regression, inheritance, fertility studies) where statistical approaches yield decisive results. Emphasises that statistics yield laws of average conduct rather than predictions for individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical predictions are about average conduct, not individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: As we can predict little or nothing of the individual atom (or vital unit), so we can predict little or nothing of the individual vital unit; we can deal only with statistics of average conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws of variation and heredity are general and definite like physics, but apply to averages. This cautions against over-interpreting individual cases; research should focus on population-level measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative criteria for studying evolution (measure variation and selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations and selection are to be quantitatively measured; the problem is to determine quantitatively the rate at which natural selection is working and has worked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply regression, measurements of heredity intensity, analyses of fertility distribution, and generational selection experiments. Example conclusions: selection for six generations can reach a permanent type with small divergence; variation and inheritance are persistent attributes that can be quantitatively characterized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure inheritance and related laws (regression and reversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of inheritance — blended and exclusive — leading respectively to the principles of regression and reversion; these factors are shown with probability to obey simple quantitative laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative treatment of inheritance, numerical examples to determine prepotency, and methods (e.g., regression analysis) to establish breeds and permanence of differences under selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical method to estimate selective vs non-selective death-rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how far inheritance of duration of life extends by correlating ages at death of related individuals (e.g., 1000 pairs of brothers) and comparing observed correlation with theoretical expectation to infer the proportion of non-selective deaths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed worked example: observed correlation between brothers' lifespans .2602 (±.0216) vs theoretical .4 gives estimated non-selective death-rate about 20% and selective about 80%. Procedure: exclude minors, form correlation table as described, compare regression slopes, and compute reduction ratio to estimate proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental and observational evidence needed for rates (not mere hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful experiments and observation are required to indicate the rapidity of the action of natural selection; natural selection is not merely hypothetical but measurable in many organisms under diverse environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages designing experiments/observational studies aimed at quantifying selection intensity and rates, and warns that such evidence will settle debates about Darwinism's reality and tempo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate classification requires collective, interdisciplinary work
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate classification could only be reached by a group of scientists having a wide appreciation of each other's fields and a thorough knowledge of their own branches of learning; they must further be endowed with sympathy and patience enough to work out a scheme in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A classification made by a single individual is likely to be suggestive but incomplete or inconsistent; a good scheme should serve as a map for lay readers and have historical and pedagogic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse material of knowledge with knowledge itself when classifying
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid failing to distinguish between the material of knowledge and knowledge itself, between the real and the ideal, or between the phenomenal world and the unreal products of metaphysical thought (a criticism leveled at Bacon's classification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sound classification must clearly delimit what counts as scientific material (sense-experience-based) and avoid mixing metaphysical categories with empirical sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be critical of hierarchical/subordination schemes without empirical basis (Comte critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comte's staircase/hierarchy that postulates subordination of sciences (mathematics→astronomy→physics→chemistry→biology→sociology→morals) is fanciful and lacks valid argument; do not limit study of a science by the requirements of the one 'above' it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifications should not artificially constrain disciplines by asserting rigid logical subordination without scientific justification; resist schematic hierarchies that misrepresent interrelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Abstract vs Concrete division (Spencer's useful starting-point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary division into Abstract Sciences (logic and mathematics, dealing with modes under which phenomena are perceived) and Concrete Sciences (those that deal with phenomena themselves) provides an excellent starting-point for classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'abstract' as conceptual space/time (conceptual tools of description) rather than perceptual empty forms; use this distinction to structure classification sensibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing classification on vague or physically unsound principles (e.g., 'redistribution of force')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not found classification schemes on vague principles that lack physical foundation (example: Spencer's 'redistribution of force' which the author finds to contradict conservation principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifying sciences on ill-defined or empirically unsupported axioms leads to unsatisfactory systems; prefer principled distinctions grounded in conceptual roles and empirical relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Occam's razor in classification and theory (Entia non sunt multiplicanda)
rubrics_metrics.description: One ought not to multiply existences beyond what are necessary to account for phenomena (Entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary duplication of conceptual entities when constructing classifications or explanatory frameworks; favour parsimonious accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification schemes should be useful and communicative to non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: A classification's scheme should be of great interest as a map of the field already covered by science and as a suggestion to the lay reader of the innumerable highways and byways by which we are reaching truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design classifications to orient both specialists and informed lay readers; historical value and pedagogic clarity are desirable properties.
